speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is confusing Singaporeans and even dividing Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All that Singaporeans want to know is why jobs and the livelihood situation for many Singaporeans have worsened over the last 20 years. "Give me the data.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Give me the answers," Singaporeans are crying out and PSP is responding to their call when we accepted the invitation from the Law Minister to do this debate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The FTAs and CECA are part of the equation when we evaluate the costs and benefits of past and present immigration and employment policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, they have to be part of this debate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a result, the PSP is strongly against the Government shutting off further discussion on the matter.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we agree that CECA is not the main issue today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In order to achieve greater economic success, Singapore always needs the right foreign talent to complement our Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSP is pro-Singaporean and welcome foreigners to work with Singaporeans for mutual benefit.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Free trade must benefit all our people and not just some people.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We want the benefits of free trade to be shared equitably with foreigners here and among all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, when there is an imbalance of interests, we would need to redress the situation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In seeking to rebalance our foreign talent policy, we are not advocating a closed Singapore nor blaming the foreigners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After all, we are responsible for our own policy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has been grappling with the foreign talent policy for the last 20 years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We take the foreign talent policy to mean all the immigration and employment policies which the Government has implemented since the late 1990s for attracting foreigners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Actually, there is not a foreign talent policy defined by the Government and debated in Parliament at the beginning.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, there was a concept of foreign talent, which was mooted in the late 1990s, in line with the idea of competition for global talent in the new knowledge-based economy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Initially, Singaporeans largely did not react negatively to it because we are basically industrious and pragmatic and ascribed to learning from others.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the Government opened the floodgates for relatively low-wage work pass holders instead of attracting foreign talent.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While Work Permit holders like the construction workers take jobs that Singaporeans generally do not want to do, the work pass holders are the Employment Pass (EP) and the S Pass (SP) holders who are collectively known as foreign PMETs because they take up jobs as professionals, managers, executives and technicians in our job market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The speed and size of the immigration due to easy immigration policies and unfair wage policies forced many Singaporeans out of jobs and then into long-term underemployment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a result, the last large displacement of Singaporean PMETs became a major issue in General Election 2011.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is unbecoming of this Government to have touted foreign talent as the reason for relaxing the immigration policies and bring in large numbers of average work pass holders instead.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, Singaporeans would like to ask the Minister for Trade and Industry to clarify further what is the definition of "foreign talent" and whether the hundreds of thousands of work pass holders in our country are all considered foreign talent.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans welcome all foreigners to complement us for mutual benefit.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, because of the potentially large numbers of average work pass holders who want a job in our country, we should have been more careful in managing the quality, number and concentration of these workers from the beginning.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The crux of the matter is that we should have been selective in taking in real foreign talent.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The failure to do was a policy failure and that is why a rebalancing is required now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I quote the then-Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean at the White Paper debate on 4 February 2013, "Singaporeans have expressed concerns over job competition, having too many foreigners and overcrowding.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We face a series of unprecedented crises in the past decade – 9/11 in 2001, SARS in 2003 and the Global Financial Crisis of 2008.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The responses we took threw our planning out of gear.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In particular, the growth in foreign workforce, total population, infrastructure and housing were not aligned.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This contributed to the anxiety, crowdedness, integration issues and the daily inconveniences faced by Singaporeans today." This was in February 2013.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the problems we are facing today are not new.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The quote from the Deputy Prime Minister then was the closest you can get from a Minister in admitting policy failures that have caused widespread hardships to many Singaporeans and Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The White Paper was to provide a roadmap to align total population, foreign workforce, infrastructure and housing based on an assumed population of 6.9 million in 2030.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government did moderate the overall workforce growth from 3% before 2013 to 2% thereafter and, belatedly, established the Fair Consideration Framework as a form of labour market testing in 2014.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the job and livelihood problem for Singaporeans did not improve and the underlying sentiments in our society continued to fester.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The issue of jobs and livelihoods resurfaced as a major issue during General Election 2020 as the finances of many Singaporeans deteriorated in the severe situation because they did not have the savings to cope with an emergency like the COVID-19 pandemic since many were displaced prior to the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We noted more committees and task forces were set up to look into the work pass holders issue after I accepted the invitation to have this debate in May.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Prime Minister has also spoken on the need to manage the quality, numbers and concentrations of foreigners in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the issues I raised are legitimate and it would be unfair if the Government continues to label PSP and I as xenophobic.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, so far, the Government only talks about tackling discrimination with legislation and does not display a full appreciation of the severity of the problem.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think that would be the main focus of our debate today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What are the causes, how serious is the problem and what are the solutions?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Legislation may not be effective because a displaced Singaporean will be in a vulnerable position and may not want to go through a long arbitration process.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Priority must be given to preventing displacement instead, and not legislation, although legislation is still welcomed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We look forward to the Government coming up with concrete measures to tackle the quality, number and concentration issues identified by the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To begin with, the Government must listen to the affected Singaporeans more patiently and then recognise the serious shortcomings of its current policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has listened to the people and has condensed their feedback in the following seven questions, which should provide invaluable insight into how we can craft the new policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Question one: why do so many Singaporeans have difficulties in finding good jobs when there are so many work pass holders in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a big imbalance in the job market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are there not enough Singaporeans or are they not given the opportunities by employers?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Question two: are there really more jobs created for Singaporeans if underemployment is a growing problem?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has maintained that there are more jobs created for Singaporeans than for work pass holders.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I know those numbers were given in the last Ministerial Statement on 6 July, but there are a lot of questions behind it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If there are insufficient jobs created, a portion of Singaporeans will become unemployed or underemployed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first type of underemployment is when a Singaporean is doing a job that does not fully utilise his most valuable skills.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, a displaced Senior Vice President of a bank may not be able to find the same replacement job and end up being a Grab driver.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second type of underemployment is when Singaporeans cannot find work for the number of hours or days she plans to do.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the low unemployment number that the Government is touting may be masking a deepening underemployment problem which we have to look into.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Question three: if there is a large pool of underemployed Singaporeans, then the shortage of talent is not due to numbers, but skills mismatch.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In that case, what has happened to our education system, world-class Universities and Polytechnics?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans are disappointed that our world-class Universities and Polytechnics were not able to produce enough talent for our key industries throughout the last 20 years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even if they are skills that Singaporeans are lacking initially, it is the responsibility of this Government to ensure that enough Singaporeans are being trained by our world-class Universities and Polytechnics.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Shortage in the first five to 10 years is acceptable, but not 20 years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, the Singaporeans would like to ask the Minister for Education, (a) what has gone wrong in the last 20 years in terms of not producing enough local talent for the finance, infocomm and professional services sectors especially; and b) what is the strategy to train Singaporeans to meet future industry needs?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Question four: by the way, what kind of skills do the average work pass holders possess that Singaporeans do not have?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have been attracting mainly the average work pass holders, judging from the low qualifying salaries for EPs and S Passes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans believe that the work pass holders are here to compete for our jobs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They do not necessarily possess unique skills, let alone create jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans would like to ask the Minister for Trade and Industry how the average work pass holders create jobs for Singaporeans, as claimed by the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Question five: if the work pass holders do not possess unique skills, then why are they dominating some of our key sectors?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore has long been a financial centre of this region and we have very conducive tax policies to promote this sector.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As we have grown with the sector, including myself, Singaporeans do not lack the skills to grow this sector further.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This situation is a far cry from what the Monetary Authority of Singapore has done for Singaporean PMETs prior to the 1990s when localisation was the norm.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans would like to ask the Minister for Trade and Industry again whether foreigners are still supposed to complement us, as the Government has always been saying, or are they here to take over us.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Question six: why has the Government allowed unfair wage competition against Singaporeans while talking about fair consideration for all?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans believe that we have arrived at our current predicament mainly because the Government has turned a blind eye towards unfair wage competition and then, later on, discrimination.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On top of that, Singaporeans have to do in-camp training.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, overall, it is more cost-effective for an employer to hire a foreigner even with their relocation and housing costs involved.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The unfair wage policies are the single most important factor behind the problems we are facing today because employers, after all, are profit seekers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This has a very debilitating effect on our Singaporean Core because, with competition and wage depression, many Singaporeans make the rational decision to avoid sectors that have competition with foreigners, like the engineering and infocomm sectors.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a result, the number of Singaporeans available to work in these sectors declined significantly over time, allowing foreigners to take up even more positions in such sectors.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a mechanism that has likely caused the rapid rise in EPs in the infocomm sector, and not because of the growth of the digital economy per se.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Question seven: why did the Government continue to consider discrimination confined to the minority of employers despite seeing the high concentration of EPs in certain sectors for the longest time?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When Singaporeans become a minority in certain sectors, Singaporeans will not be the first to be considered when new opportunities arise.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The infocomm sector is a case in point, where many new jobs have gone to more newly arrived work pass holders each year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Based on feedback from many Singaporeans, the number of work pass holders is large enough and they have been here long enough to have formed networks among main contractors, outsourcing vendors, recruitment agencies, HR managers and even top managers, which discriminate against Singaporean workers in their hiring practices.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat shared an episode recently, quote, "A Singaporean who attended a job interview at an MNC was asked by the foreign HR manager, 'You wrote in your CV that you spent two years with the SAF.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is SAF?' This HR manager exemplified all that is wrong with our immigration and employment policies for allowing a foreigner who has little knowledge about the local job culture to be in a decision-making position." No male Singaporean jobseeker should be made to go through this kind of insult again.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After all has been said, this Government needs to remember that having a job that commensurates with one's ability is the foundation of human dignity, and income stability is important for families to have a conducive environment for the children.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the breadwinner is out of job or does not earn enough, a host of social problems will arise.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a Japanese saying, "Every child grows up while watching the back of his father." What this means is that if the father is doing well, he is likely to stand tall and look confident, and that will have a positive influence on the child.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, if a father is unemployed, his posture is stooped and self-assurance is low and that will have a negative influence on the child.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Every time a resident relates his displacement story to me, my initial response is one of anger, but later I will cry when I see the effect on his family and children.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Each such encounter stiffens my resolve to make Singapore a more compassionate society and to give each child a good childhood.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have debated the same issues in February 2013 at the Population White Paper debate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But Singaporeans' jobs and livelihoods did not improve after that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government says we have not enough talents.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But there are many underemployed Singaporeans and we have a world-class education system with world-class Universities and Polytechnics.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Government says the jobs require skills that Singaporeans do not have.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But do you mean so many Singaporeans cannot do the job of those average work pass holders?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Government says discrimination is confined to a minority but do you not see the concentrations in companies, industries and workplaces?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The whole situation gave the impression that this Government is not well-coordinated within itself.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Each Ministry may be trying to do its best, but the whole Government is not aligned to achieve the best outcome.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The misalignment that Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean spoke of at the Population White Paper debate in 2013 seems not to be resolved yet.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today's debate continues to be handicapped by the Government's unwillingness to give full disclosure on immigration and employment data.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not just restricted to the nationality data, but a lot of other data.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have filed a total of 23 Parliamentary Questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The debate was further hindered by unnecessary distraction like comments about racial undertones.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Motion tabled by the Government did not reflect a full appreciation of the severity of the problem arising from the over presence of work pass holders.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Neither does it contain substantial and concrete ideas to resolve the problem.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we pass this Government Motion, the debate today will very likely become another Population White Paper debate of 2013.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the PSP calls for urgent and concrete measures to be implemented immediately to restore some balance in our job market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These will create a better chance for our new graduates of getting good jobs and older PMETs of retaining their jobs immediately.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We think new laws may not be effective because a displaced Singaporean will not be in a strong position to go through a legal or arbitration process.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also aim for 25% to 30% combined PMET cap on work pass holders and PRs in the long run.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: New companies can be allowed to deviate from the cap provided they can prove there is a genuine shortage of such skills in Singapore and they have concrete and committed plans for localisation, including transference of knowledge and skills within a stipulated time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also recommend the creation of Standing Select Committees for every Ministry in this Parliament with representatives from different parties to enable more informative exchange on policies and monitor the implementation of new policies until the anxieties of our Singaporeans are completely relieved.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not forget those Singaporeans who have been displaced too.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not only help them look for a good replacement job, but also give financial help for the healthcare and education needs of their family during the period when they are underemployed, especially we should not allow a problem of this generation to have a long-term negative effect on the next generation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSP has given careful consideration and felt it is our duty to raise the issue, file this Motion and have it fully debated.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans can see that the Government is taking this issue more front and centre in its public pronouncements, including in the 2021 National Day Rally.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This must be the start of a healthy and proper dialogue.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans deserve better – for country, for people.
